sum: Abbott Laboratories announced two product developments on Tuesday, November 10, spanning consumer diagnostics and cardiac devices. The updates add regulatory and product milestones as investors assess the healthcare group's pipeline.

Abbott introduced a new Panbio COVID-19/Flu A&B self-test for Canadian families during the respiratory illness season. The product is positioned to support at-home testing for both COVID-19 and influenza A and B.

The company also announced FDA approval and CE marking for an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator lead designed to work with the heart's natural electrical system. The milestone strengthens Abbott's presence in cardiac rhythm management, where product approvals can shape the pace of portfolio expansion.
The announcements were listed in Abbott's MediaRoom on November 10.

The self-test addresses seasonal respiratory diagnostics, while the cardiac lead targets a more specialized medical-device market. Together, the releases show Abbott advancing products with different regulatory and commercial profiles rather than relying on a single pipeline catalyst.

Should You Buy, Hold or Sell Abbott Stock Post-Q3 Earnings?
sum: Abbott ABT delivered a stronger top- and bottom-line performance in the third quarter of 2026. Sales increased 14.5% year over year to $13.01 billion and surpassed the Zacks Consensus Estimate by 0.3%. Adjusted earnings per share (EPS) of $1.42 rose 9.2% from the prior-year quarter but fell short of the consensus mark by 0.7%. Among segments, Established Pharmaceuticals (“EPD”) delivered broad-based growth across geographies and therapeutic areas. Medical Devices benefited from double-digit growth in Electrophysiology and Rhythm Management, while Diagnostics gained from strong Core Laboratory testing demand and continued momentum in Cancer Diagnostics.

Alongside the quarterly results, Abbott also announced plans to separate its global Nutrition business into an independent, publicly traded company following a comprehensive strategic review. The move is designed to give each business greater strategic and operational focus, improve resource allocation and enhance commercial and R&D execution. The transaction is expected to be completed by the end of 2027, subject to customary conditions and final approval by Abbott's Board of Directors.

After the separation, Abbott expects to have approximately $42 billion in sales and leading positions across cardiovascular and neuromodulation devices, biowearables, laboratory, point-of-care and cancer diagnostics, and established medicines.

Abbott’s stock has gained 6.7% since the release of third-quarter 2026 earnings on Oct. 21. Over the past six months, shares have risen 28.4%, outpacing the broader Medical sector and the S&P 500. The stock also fared much better than peers Intuitive Surgical ISRG and ResMed RMD, whose shares gained 2.8% and 18%, respectively.

Within Diagnostics, Core Lab sales grew 5.5% year over year, driven by strong performance in the United States, Europe, Japan, and Latin America. Management noted that testing data from thousands of instruments across the United States and global markets continued to point to healthy, stable demand in the third quarter, consistent with the trend observed in July. Meanwhile, Cancer diagnostics growth of 14% was led by Cologuard, with contributions from Abbott’s Precision Oncology and international businesses.

Warren Buffett Says His Favorite Holding Period Is Forever. A Secretary Who Paid $180 for 3 Shares in 1935 and Never Sold Died Worth $7 Million. Here's What Her Rule Does for $600,000 in One Stock Today
sum: Warren Buffett Says His Favorite Holding Period Is Forever. A Secretary Who Paid $180 for 3 Shares in 1935 and Never Sold Died Worth $7 Million. Here’s What Her Rule Does for $600,000 in One Stock Today
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.

Warren Buffett wrote in his 1988 letter to Berkshire Hathaway shareholders that "when we own portions of outstanding businesses with outstanding managements, our favorite holding period is forever." The best proof of that rule was a secretary in Lake Forest, Illinois, named Grace Groner. In 1935 she paid $180 for three shares of Abbott Laboratories, the company that employed her. She never sold a share and reinvested every dividend. When she died in January 2010 at 100, her estate came to $7 million, and she left it all to Lake Forest College, her alma mater, through a foundation she had set up for the purpose.

The Chicago Tribune told her story in March 2010: 43 years as a secretary at Abbott, a one-bedroom cottage that had been willed to her, clothes from rummage sales, no car. "Oh, my God," the college’s president, Stephen Schutt, said when he learned the amount. About 1,300 students have since taken internships and study abroad on her money.

Her $7 million reads as the strongest case anyone has made for Buffett’s rule that the best holding period is forever, and the limit of that reading is that she held one company that kept raising its dividend for 54 straight years, so the rule only did its work because the company did. Here is what her $180 became, where the money came from, what the same rule costs, and what it would do for a reader holding one old stock today.

Three shares at $60 in 1935, $7 million in January 2010: that is a multiple of 38,889 times over 75 years, or 15.1% a year compounded. The same $180 in the S&P 500 with every dividend reinvested, from the start of 1935 through the end of 2009, would have grown to about $341,282, by Damodaran’s annual return series at NYU Stern, which is 10.6% a year. She beat the index 21 times over.
The part most retellings skip is where the money came from.

Ives Puts a 20%-25% 'Political Discount' on SpaceX Stock, Still Sees Tesla Deal
sum: SpaceX shares are trading at a political markdown of as much as a quarter of their value, according to Wedbush analyst Dan Ives, who nonetheless expects the rocket-and-satellite group to eventually absorb Tesla.

Ives told Anthony Pompliano on The Pomp Podcast that the midterm elections have made SpaceX's expansion harder, particularly in Texas, where much of its data-center buildout is planned. He estimated the political overhang at 20% to 25% of the stock's value.

"I still believe SpaceX acquires Tesla," Ives said, while cautioning that the path to a combination now carries more obstacles. He argued that Chief Executive Elon Musk cannot simply relocate the projects to Florida and predicted the billionaire will negotiate with Texas officials. "He will come to the table. I do think the negotiation will happen," he said.

The political backdrop shifted sharply in last week's vote. Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat who unseated Governor Greg Abbott, campaigned on an immediate pause in new data-center construction until lawmakers write stronger protections for host communities, and has said she is willing to work with Musk's companies on her administration's terms. Abbott had already ordered a halt to data-center permits in September pending audits of power and water needs.

Against that resistance, SpaceX is seeking a property tax abatement for a planned gas-fired power plant and supercomputing campus at Starbase, its launch site on the Gulf Coast. A public hearing notice puts the estimated investment for the first phase at $24 billion, ranking it among the largest private projects ever proposed in the Rio Grande Valley. The Starbase City Commission is scheduled to take up the abatement and a related economic development agreement at a public meeting on Dec. 9.

The notice did not disclose the plant's generating capacity, the size of the computing installation, or the length and value of the tax relief being requested. SpaceX would build, own and operate the infrastructure, and generating its own electricity could spare it a lengthy wait for a connection to the state's main grid. The power could also serve the large semiconductor plant SpaceX is developing with Tesla in Grimes County.

What Does Abbott’s (NYSE:ABT) Formula Settlement Mean Now?
sum: - Abbott agreed to resolve federal and state claims tied to its in earlier years infant formula recall.

Abbott Laboratories (NYSE:ABT) Healthcare Abbott Laboratories (NYSE:ABT) 109.93 USD -0.030 0.027% Last Updated at: 2026-11-06T21:02:00Z , the diversified healthcare group known for devices, diagnostics, nutrition and branded medicines, announced an agreement that draws a line under one of the most closely watched legal episodes in its recent history. Those several statements are central to how the news was received, because they affect both the legal and the reputational dimensions.

According to the company's own announcement, issued from its Illinois headquarters, the payment resolves several parallel tracks at once. By packaging them together, Abbott avoids having to litigate in multiple forums that could otherwise run for years and produce inconsistent outcomes. The announcement also states that the settlement is not an admission. That phrase is standard in negotiated resolutions, where defendants agree to pay to end uncertainty while denying wrongdoing. Observers pay attention to what is excluded as well as what is included, and the release does not describe the specific legal theories behind the claims.

The dispute traces to early in earlier years, when Abbott recalled certain powdered infant formulas made at its Sturgis plant after releases of infant illnesses and concern over possible bacterial contamination. The recall, combined with the shutdown of the facility for a period, contributed to a nationwide shortage that affected families, hospitals and retailers and became a political issue in Washington. The shortage prompted emergency regulatory measures and congressional hearings and left lasting scars on the infant nutrition market. Parents who had relied on specific products were forced to switch, and the episode revealed how concentrated domestic supply had become.

Abbott used its announcement to restate its position on the underlying facts. It says no unopened, distributed Abbott infant formula has ever tested positive for the group bacteria at issue, Cronobacter sakazakii or Salmonella Newport.

sum: President Donald Trump has sparked fresh controversy by sharing a series of posts questioning the results of the midterm elections, including Democrat James Talarico's stunning victory in Texas – just days after promising to accept the outcome.

The president spent part of Saturday amplifying claims about 'unusual' voting patterns, dramatic increases in Democratic support and election-night figures that some conservative commentators suggested were difficult to believe.

Trump shared several charts and messages on Truth Social that appeared to cast doubt on the scale of the Democrats' sweeping victories, which saw Republicans lose control of both chambers of Congress.
But none of the material he circulated provided evidence of election fraud or wrongdoing.

The posts mark a striking change in tone from Tuesday night, when Trump told The New York Times he was 'absolutely willing' to accept the election results and work with the incoming Democratic majorities.
One of the most provocative messages concerned Talarico's crushing victory over Trump-backed Republican Ken Paxton in the Texas Senate race.
The president reposted a message from an account called The Lone Raccoon, which featured a graph showing the candidates' vote totals rising throughout election night, including several sharp jumps.

People still need syringes, glucose sensors, and replacement hips when the economy slows, and that steady demand is what lets the largest medical device makers keep raising their dividends. Abbott Laboratories (NYSE:ABT | ABT Price Prediction), Stryker (NYSE:SYK) and Becton Dickinson (NYSE:BDX) all turn that demand into a growing income stream. Abbott Laboratories: 54 Years of Raises and a Promise of More

Abbott makes continuous glucose monitors for diabetics, heart rhythm devices, diagnostic tests, nutrition products, and branded generic drugs. With a recent share price of $110.50, the stock yields 2.18% on an annual dividend of $2.52 per share.

Dividend safety: Abbott’s record is about as strong as it gets. Billionaire Musk’s Tesla, SpaceX tumble in post-US midterm AI meltdown
sum: Shares of Elon Musk-led companies plunged on Nov 5, deepening a rout that began after Democrats outperformed in the US midterm elections, as investors worry the billionaire’s efforts to expand his business empire will be stymied.

Tesla shares sank 11% on Nov 5, following a 3.3% drop a day earlier. For the year, Tesla shares are now down about 24%. SpaceX, Musk’s rocket, satellite and AI company, tumbled 9% on Nov 5 on the back of a 3.8% decline the day before.
Since the results became clear, Tesla and SpaceX shares have sloughed off roughly US$460 billion (S$588 billion) from their combined market value.

“Tesla and SpaceX are just a 2-for-1 special as the market attempts to reprice the risk of a material slowing in data centre buildouts,” said Joe Gilbert, portfolio manager at Integrity Asset Management. “Momentum is a powerful thing that cuts both ways and there is a rush to the exits in tech until we see some kind of bottoming.”
Democrats seized key positions in Musk’s home state of Texas, where Tesla and SpaceX have their headquarters, and won a majority of seats in both chambers of Congress.
The Texas results were a particular focal point, with Gina Hinojosa ousting Governor Greg Abbott, the Republican who had held the state’s highest office since 2015.

On the campaign trail, Hinojosa called for a moratorium on data centres and cast scrutiny on Musk’s political contributions to Abbott, as well as state tax breaks provided to Musk companies during Abbott’s tenure.

From debilitating to relief: Athlete shares battle with Complex Regional Pain Syndrome
sum: (Rockford News First) - Shae Eichele-Gawry, a former competitive cheerleader and gymnast, never imagined a routine stunt would lead to a life-altering injury.
After performing an advanced rewind stunt as a flyer, she injured her leg and ankle. Despite numerous surgeries, treatments and physical therapy, Shae lived in constant pain.
It took more than two years to receive a diagnosis: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS), widely considered one of the world’s most painful chronic conditions.
CRPS affects more than 200,000 people in the U.S. each year. It occurs when the body overreacts to an injury or surgery, causing intense, worsening pain and extreme inflammation.

On Wednesday, Rockford News First anchor Alyssa Kelly talked with Shae and Dr. Allen Burton, divisional vice president and chief medical officer of Abbott’s neuromodulation business - the team behind the technology that changed Shae’s life.
Shae found lasting relief through the Abbott Proclaim DRG System, which delivers electrical pulses to a specific cluster of nerves along the spine to block pain signals before they reach the brain.
Today, Shae is an award-winning bodybuilder, celebrating major personal milestones and back to living an active lifestyle.

sum: It's looking like the election might become even more expensive for Elon Musk.
Shares in Tesla and SpaceX fell more than 4% premarket on Wednesday after the Democrats won a string of midterm victories in Texas, where both companies are based.

The Texas results, which saw James Talarico beat Republican nominee Ken Paxton to the Senate seat and Democratic candidate Gina Hinojosa unseat longtime governor Greg Abbott, will be especially painful for Musk.
The Tesla and SpaceX CEO spent roughly $224 million backing Republican candidates in Texas, according to The New York Times, including $158 million in September alone.
Should the share drops for SpaceX and Tesla hold at market open, Musk's companies could lose more than $140 billion in combined market value.
Musk, who moved SpaceX's HQ from California in 2024 after criticizing the state's lawmakers, now faces the prospect of his two public companies once again being regulated by Democratic officials.

Texas is the home of Tesla's Austin gigafactory, and the company's robotaxi service operates in multiple cities across the state. SpaceX, meanwhile, launches its Starship rocket from its Starbase facility in Boca Chica, near the Mexican border.

sum: HONG KONG – A morning rally for U.S. stocks petered out on Monday as the tech and AI industries remained shaky following their sell-off last week.
The S&P 500 sank 0.5% after erasing a gain that had reached 1.1% early in the day. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 213 points, or 0.4%, while the Nasdaq composite fell 1.1%.

The mixed performance for indexes came even though the majority of stocks within the S&P 500 climbed. They benefited from a 7.6% drop for the price of a barrel of Brent crude to $104.77. It’s the latest yo-yo move for oil prices on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the global industry to return to normal.

The price for the most actively traded contract in the Brent market has been veering between roughly $70 and $120 per barrel since just before the war with Iran began, and it’s been quick to reverse direction.

So have stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry, which have been shaky for months amid criticism that they surged too high and are in a bubble. Worries are growing that all the hundreds of billions of dollars Big Tech companies are pouring into AI data centers won’t yield enough productivity and profit to make the investments worth it.

The latest profit reports from Alphabet and other Big Tech companies also showed how AI may be dragging on their own businesses. Not only did Google’s parent company burn through more cash during the latest quarter, as measured by something called free cash flow, it also reported slower-than-expected growth in its search business, which raised worries about AI undercutting its cash cow. That caused Alphabet’s stock to drop more than 12% Thursday for its worst day on record.

On Monday, Alphabet initially rallied 2.6%, but it later erased the gain and then finished with a loss of 0.3%. Nvidia, meanwhile, went from an early gain of 2.6% to a drop of 1.3% following its 4.2% slide on Friday. Such swings dragged the rest of the market with them.

Medtronic Just Retired 55 Million Shares Without Spending Cash. Is the Stock a Buy?
sum: Medtronic (MDT +2.85%) is entering new waters after spinning off its diabetes segment, now called MiniMed (MMED +3.39%). The hope for the medical devices company is that the move will unlock greater margins.

Investors have been a bit dubious about the stock, despite strong financials. It's down just under 1% so far this year, but over the last three months, it has climbed more than 11%. Here are three reasons why Medtronic might be a buy.
The list of Dividend Kings is a small one. Out of roughly 7,000 stocks on major U.S. exchanges, only 59 have made it to the list by increasing their dividends for 50 or more consecutive years.

Companies on that list have survived multiple recessions and market crashes, all while maintaining cash-flow stability and market competitiveness. It's an elite list that investors pay attention to, and Medtronic has increased its dividend for 49 consecutive years, including a 1.4% increase in 2026. If it raises its dividend in 2027, as expected, the milestone will likely boost stock sales as institutional inflows and fund rebalancing increase.
The company's trailing cash dividend payout ratio is just under 60%, leaving plenty of room for additional dividend increases.

In the first quarter of fiscal 2027 -- the quarter ended July 31 -- Medtronic reported revenue of $9.8 billion, up nearly 14%, year over year. The bump was led by the company's cardiovascular segment, in which revenue rose by 19% over the same period last year. The company's two remaining segments, neuroscience and medical surgical, saw revenue rise 14% and 9%, respectively.

EPS rose 15%, year over year, to $1.45. Medtronic had previously forecast yearly organic revenue to increase between 7.25% and 7.75%, and for yearly EPS to rise between 7.4% and 8.5%. However, the guidance was released before the company's MiniMed spinoff, so those numbers will change.

Abbott Laboratories reported third-quarter revenue of $13.013 billion, beating the analyst consensus estimate of $12.998 billion by 0.12%. The company’s adjusted earnings per share (EPS) came in at $1.42, meeting the consensus estimate of $1.41.

This performance represents a 14.46% increase in sales compared to the $11.369 billion reported in the same period last year. Adjusted EPS rose 9.23% from $1.30 per share in the year-ago quarter. Shares of Abbott fell 0.8% to close at $104.06 on Monday, ahead of the release.

The top-line growth of 14.46% significantly outpaced the 9.23% growth in adjusted EPS, indicating that while revenue expanded robustly, profitability gains were more moderate relative to sales expansion. The slight beat on revenue suggests stronger-than-expected demand or operational efficiency during the quarter.

With the recent buzz around Abbott, some investors may be eyeing potential gains from the company’s dividends. As of now, Abbott has an annual dividend yield of 2.42%, which equates to a quarterly dividend amount of 63 cents per share ($2.52 a year).

To earn $500 per month or $6,000 annually from dividends alone, an investor would need an investment of approximately $247,767 or around 2,381 shares. For a more modest $100 per month or $1,200 per year, the requirement is $49,533 or around 476 shares.

sum: Abbott Laboratories (NYSE:ABT) shares rose nearly 11% on Thursday after the healthcare company reported second quarter 2026 results that topped Wall Street expectations and raised its full-year adjusted earnings guidance.
The company posted adjusted diluted earnings per share of $1.31 for the quarter, ahead of analyst expectations of $1.28.
Revenue came in at $12.59 billion, slightly above the consensus estimate of $12.52 billion and up 13% on a reported basis from the prior-year period.

On a comparable basis, which excludes the impact of foreign exchange and other specified items, sales increased 4.8% in the second quarter. Abbott reaffirmed its full-year 2026 comparable sales growth outlook of 6.5% to 7.5%.
The company raised its full-year adjusted diluted EPS guidance to a range of $5.45 to $5.60, compared with its previous outlook of $5.38 to $5.58.
Abbott expects third quarter adjusted diluted EPS of $1.38 to $1.46.

"Our second-quarter results reflect the momentum we are building," Abbott CEO Robert Ford said in a statement. "We expect this momentum to continue and drive accelerating sales and earnings growth in the second half of the year."

sum: Daily news & progressive opinion—funded by the people, not the corporations—delivered straight to your inbox.
Abbott, which donated $500,000 to the president's inaugural fund, faced an investigation stemming from alleged deadly contamination at one of its baby formula plants in Michigan.

US President Donald Trump last year purchased hundreds of thousands of dollars of Abbott Laboratories stock before his Justice Department dropped a years-long criminal investigation into the company, which was accused of misconduct after infant hospitalizations and deaths were linked to one of its baby formula factories.

The stock purchases were revealed in the president's annual financial disclosure report, which spans 927 pages and shows thousands of trades valued at over $1 billion. Trump's first purchase of Abbott stock last year was made in late September, and the president bought around $500,000 worth of shares in total in 2025, according to the nonprofit media organization More Perfect Union.

The Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday that "top decision makers" at the Department of Justice shut down the criminal investigation into Abbott—which donated $500,000 to Trump's inaugural fund—even though "some prosecutors believed they had evidence to criminally charge the company under a law they have used to pursue other businesses for allegedly selling contaminated foods."

"Prosecutors had been considering a misdemeanor charge against Abbott for violating the federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and a separate count for misleading the government," the Journal reported, citing unnamed people familiar with the matter. "Investigators in early 2022 had found traces of a potentially deadly bacteria at its plant in Sturgis, Michigan, including on equipment very close to infant formula containers—as well as a long list of other problems."

The Food and Drug Administration received reports of at least nine infant deaths linked to baby formula produced at Abbott's Sturgis plant, which the company temporarily shut down amid fears of dangerous contamination. The Justice Department launched its investigation into Abbott, the largest infant formula manufacturer in the US, in 2023, under the administration of former President Joe Biden.

Although media reports or rumors about a significant change in a company's business prospects usually cause its stock to trend and lead to an immediate price change, there are always certain fundamental factors that ultimately drive the buy-and-hold decision.

Here at Zacks, we prioritize appraising the change in the projection of a company's future earnings over anything else. That's because we believe the present value of its future stream of earnings is what determines the fair value for its stock.

We essentially look at how sell-side analysts covering the stock are revising their earnings estimates to reflect the impact of the latest business trends. And if earnings estimates go up for a company, the fair value for its stock goes up. A higher fair value than the current market price drives investors' interest in buying the stock, leading to its price moving higher. sum: MiniMed (Nasdaq:MMED) announced today that it expanded its agreement with Abbott (NYSE:ABT) to add more sensors to its portfolio.
The company also announced fourth-quarter earnings results in tandem with the new Abbott integration.

MiniMed has an existing partnership with Abbott through a collaboration between the companies agreed in 2024. They integrated Instinct, a sensor made by Abbott and based on the FreeStyle Libre platform, into Medtronic insulin delivery offerings.

Now, the companies plan to commercialize dual glucose-ketone sensors and integrate them with MiniMed smart dosing systems. Abbott has long touted the dual sensor that continuously measures glucose and ketone levels every minute. The sensors provide real-time visibility into glucose levels as a standard CGM like Abbott’s FreeStyle Libre system does, but also into rising ketones that can lead to a diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) emergency.
Last week, Abbott reached a milestone with CE mark for the sensors, branded as Libre Duo and Libre Duo 10 Day. The sensors remain investigational in the U.S.

MiniMed plans to offer the sensors across its automated insulin delivery and smart multiple daily injection (MDI) systems. The sensors will be the same size as Instinct. The companies plan to provide further updates on regulatory and commercialization milestones in the coming months.

“By integrating dual glucose-ketone monitoring sensors with our MiniMed smart dosing systems, we’re adding an additional layer of intelligence and protection,” said Que Dallara, CEO. “Our system is designed to keep people in tight glucose control and minimize DKA risk through smarter, more consistent automation — intervening before it ever becomes an emergency. This partnership with Abbott takes that commitment even further. At MiniMed, our mission is to make every day a better day for people with diabetes, and that means relentlessly pursuing innovations that not only improve outcomes but also deliver genuine peace of mind.”

In 4Q, Abbott's sales were US$11.5 billion, below the average analyst estimate of US$11.8 billion. Adjusted earnings in the quarter were US$1.50 a share, matching what Wall Street expected. Nutrition sales were US$1.9 billion, far short of the average analyst estimate of US$2.19 billion.
The shares fell 5.6% in Thursday premarket trading in New York. The stock rose 3.4% in the 12 months through Wednesday's close, while the S&P 500 index gained 14%.

Abbott sells a wide variety of products from medical devices to baby formula, as well as nutrition products for adults. Its adult nutrition unit, which includes protein-focused drinks for people on weight-loss drugs, has grown in recent quarters. However, Abbott's infant products have also been mired in controversy following lawsuits alleging its formula can cause necrotising enterocolitis, or NEC, a serious bowel ailment that affects premature babies.

Medical device sales, Abbott's largest business unit, totalled US$5.67 billion in 4Q, in line with estimates. The devision sells tools that help diabetics monitor blood sugar, such as continuous glucose monitors.

items.t: Exact Sciences stock jumps after Abbott confirms acquisition
sum: Investing.com -- Exact Sciences (NASDAQ:EXAS) stock soared 17% Thursday, building on Wednesday's 24% surge after Abbott (NYSE:ABT) announced plans to acquire the cancer diagnostics company in a deal valued at approximately $21 billion.

The Madison, Wisconsin-based company's shares traded at $101 in pre-market trading, following yesterday's close of $86.18, which had already jumped 23.68% amid Bloomberg-reported acquisition rumors that have now been confirmed.

Under the agreement terms, Exact Sciences shareholders will receive $105 per share in cash, representing a premium that appears to have exceeded market expectations. The acquisition values Exact Sciences at an enterprise value of approximately $23 billion, including the company's estimated $1.8 billion in net debt.

The deal will position Abbott to enter the fast-growing $60 billion U.S. cancer screening and precision oncology diagnostics market. Exact Sciences, projected to generate over $3 billion in revenue this year with high teens organic sales growth, brings its market-leading Cologuard colorectal cancer screening test and Oncotype DX precision oncology test to Abbott's portfolio.

Abbott expects the acquisition to be immediately accretive to its revenue growth and gross margin. Following the completion of the transaction, expected in the second quarter of 2026, Exact Sciences will become a subsidiary of Abbott, pushing Abbott's total diagnostics sales beyond $12 billion annually.
The transaction, unanimously approved by both companies' boards of directors, remains subject to Exact Sciences shareholder approval and regulatory clearances.
